sections.text: In this capstone we build a small text adventure: rooms you walk between, a key to find, and a locked vault to open. A real game would read what you type. This app has no keyboard input for programs, so the commands come from a list in main instead. Everything else works exactly like the real thing.

First, the commands. We turn each line of text into a Command enum, so the rest of the game works with proper values instead of strings. Directions are their own enum. #[derive(...)] asks the compiler to write standard trait implementations for you: Clone and Copy let us copy a Direction freely, and PartialEq, Eq and Hash let us use it as a HashMap key later.

Next, the world. Each Room has a description, a map of exits (a Direction leads to the name of another room) and maybe an item lying there. Option<&'static str> means "maybe some text"; &'static str is a string literal written straight into the program. All rooms live in a HashMap, so we can look one up by name.

The game itself is a state machine: at any moment it is in exactly one State, and each command may move it to another. Here the state is Playing until you enter the vault, and then Won. The Game struct holds the whole situation: the rooms, where you are, what you carry, and the state. Its step method takes one Command, changes the game, and returns the text to show.

Follow the script: the first go west fails because the vault is locked. The player walks north, takes the key, comes back, and the second go west wins. Because step checks the inventory, the rules of the game live in one place. To grow the game, add a room to Game::new, a variant to Command, or a new arm in step. The compiler will point out every match you forgot to update.
Why use enums here instead of strings everywhere? A string like "go wset" can hide a typo. A Command::Go(Direction::West) cannot be misspelled, and match makes you handle every case.

This is a simple state machine in the type-driven style: the Command enum models input, State models the phase, and match forces every combination to be handled. The same shape fits parsers, protocol handlers and UI flows. Inventory strings could become an enum Item, and rooms could be addressed by an enum RoomId instead of &'static str, so a typo in a room name becomes a compile error rather than a runtime panic in the HashMap lookup.

exercise.prompt: The parse function does not know the word "i" yet. Add "inventory" | "i" => Command::Inventory to the match, where | means "or". The program should print three lines: You see a dusty hall., You carry: key, lamp, I don't understand 'dance'.
exercise.expectedOutput:
You see a dusty hall.
You carry: key, lamp
I don't understand 'dance'.

quiz.question: Why are the rooms stored in a HashMap?
options: HashMap keeps them in alphabetical order
We can look a room up by its name
Rooms can't be stored in a Vec

quiz.question: In parse, what does the last arm _ => Command::Unknown(...) do?
options: Catches every input that no earlier arm matched

quiz.question: What does the State enum model?
options: The phase the game is in: exactly one of Playing or Won at a time
